Field surveys of Mannophryne trinitatis across the montane streams of Trinidad's Northern Range have provided detailed morphometric data for both sexes. Adult females attain a maximum snout-vent length of 2.55 cm [Li = 2.55 cm], a value notably larger than the 2.2 cm figure sometimes cited in earlier field guides, likely reflecting the inclusion of fully gravid individuals in the present sample. Males, by contrast, reach a smaller ultimate snout-vent length of 2.0 cm [Li = 2.0 cm], a pattern of sexual size dimorphism consistent with the reproductive ecology of many dendrobatid frogs, where larger females accommodate greater clutch volumes. The smallest post-metamorphic individuals encountered during the surveys measured approximately 1.1 cm  in snout-vent length, and given their recently resorbed tail stubs and incomplete adult coloration, these were interpreted as females that had just completed metamorphosis and emerged from the streamside nurseries. This small body size at the terrestrial juvenile stage underscores the substantial growth trajectory that individuals must undergo before reaching reproductive maturity.

Reproductive biology in Mannophryne trinitatis is tightly coupled to the thermal conditions of the headwater streams it inhabits. At a constant water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], females produce between 2 and 12 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 12 eggs per clutch], with a single clutch deposited each year [F_R_i = single clutch deposited each year], a modest reproductive output that aligns with the extended parental care typical of the genus. Under the same thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum achievable reproductive rate is approximately 12 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 12 eggs per year]. Embryonic development proceeds within gelatinous egg masses attached to submerged leaf litter, and the duration of the incubation period is strongly influenced by stream temperature; field measurements at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] indicate that eggs hatch after approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days], a period consistent with the lower end of the 17- to 26-day range reported for captive populations.

Neonatal life history traits in this species reflect adaptations to the nutrient-poor, oxygen-saturated waters of its montane habitat. At the moment of hatching, each newly emerged larva weighs approximately 0.0224 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0224 grams], a mass derived directly from the 3.5 mm egg diameter, corresponding to a spherical yolk reserve that provides the sole nutritional substrate during the early lecithotrophic phase. Hatchlings remain attached to the jelly of the egg mass for several days, absorbing the remaining yolk before commencing exogenous feeding. At the same developmental temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], these yolk-sac larvae undergo a predictable sequence of morphological changes: mouthparts develop, the operculum forms, and the transition to active filter feeding begins. The tiny body mass at emergence places considerable constraints on the initial growth rate, as the larvae must locate suitable algal grazing patches within the stream environment before their endogenous yolk reserves are fully depleted.

As the aquatic tadpoles develop and approach metamorphic climax, the body plan undergoes dramatic reorganisation, culminating in the emergence of a terrestrial juvenile froglet. For females, the ultimate wet weight attained by reproductively active adults is 1.9 grams [Wwi = 1.9 grams], a body mass that is achieved after a prolonged period of terrestrial growth and feeding on small invertebrates such as ants, mites, and springtails. Under the thermal conditions of the streamside environment maintained at a mean of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the interval from metamorphosis to the onset of gonadal maturation spans approximately 56 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 56 days following metamorphosis]. This relatively brief period of post-metamorphic development before reproductive activation suggests that individuals allocate resources rapidly toward somatic growth immediately after the larval-juvenile transition, enabling them to enter the breeding population within the same season if conditions remain favorable.

Longevity records for Mannophryne trinitatis in the wild remain sparse, but mark-recapture studies conducted over a five-year period in the Arima Valley provide an estimated maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] for individuals inhabiting stable, undisturbed stream reaches at an average temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This lifespan, while modest by amphibian standards, is comparable to that reported for other small-bodied dendrobatids in the Trinidadian highlands and reflects a life-history strategy that balances a relatively low annual reproductive output with extended parental investment. Males guard the egg clutches and transport the newly hatched tadpoles on their backs to isolated pools, a behavior that reduces predation risk but imposes energetic costs that may contribute to the observed longevity ceiling. Senescence in older individuals is marked by reduced skin turgor, slower escape responses, and decreased feeding efficiency, leading to gradual declines in body condition before eventual mortality.
